Name: Rho GTPase activation protein
ShortDescription: Proteins containing a RhoGAP (Rho GTPase Activating Protein) domain usually function to catalyse the hydrolysis of GTP that is bound to Rho, Rac and/or Cdc42, inactivating these regulators of the actin cytoskeleton. The 53 known human RhoGAP domain-containing proteins are the largest known group of Rho GTPase regulators and significantly outnumber the 21 Rho GTPases they presumably regulate. This excess of GAP proteins probably indicates complex regulation of the Rho GTPases and is consistent with the existence of almost as many (48) human Dbl domain-containing Rho GEFs that act antagonistically to the RhoGAP proteins by activating the Rho GTPases. Phylogenetic analysis offers evidence for frequent domain duplication and for duplication of the entire genes containing these GAP domains [[cite:PUB00010623]].

Name: Histone chaperone domain CHZ
ShortDescription: This domain is highly conserved from yeasts to humans and is part of the chaperone protein HIRIP3 in vertebrates which interacts with the H3.3 chaperone HIRA, implicated in histone replacement during transcription. N- and C- termini of Chz family members are relatively divergent but do contain similar acidic stretches rich in Glu/Asp residues, characteristic of all histone chaperones [[cite:PUB00044198]].

Name: BING4, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This C-terminal domain is found in the BING4 family of nucleolar WD40 repeat proteins [[cite:PUB00016366]].

Name: WD repeat-containing protein WDR46/Utp7
ShortDescription: This entry contains proteins with a BING4-like, C-terminal domain. WD repeat-containing protein 46 (WDR46) is a component of the nuclear scaffold, which is an insoluble structure that contributes to the inner nuclear organization. WDR46 is a fundamental scaffold component of the nucleolar structure, binding nucleolin and DDX21 [[cite:PUB00090808]]. Also in this family is U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 7 (UTP7) from baker's yeast, which is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]].

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 18
ShortDescription: Utp18 is a small-subunit (SSU) processome protein involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and ribosome assembly [[cite:PUB00035836]].

Name: Regulator of rDNA transcription 14
ShortDescription: Rrt14 is a nucleolar protein whose function is not clear. It was identified in a screen for mutants with decreased levels of rDNA transcription [[cite:PUB00075791]]. It may be involved in ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00075792]].

Name: UTP25, NTP hydrolase-like domain
ShortDescription:
UTP25 (U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 25) is a DEAD-box RNA helicase-like protein component of the ribosomal small subunit processome for the biogenesis of ribosomes, which functions in pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) processing [[cite:PUB00109164]]. U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 25 homologue (UTP25, also known as Digestive organ expansion factor (DEF)) from animals is essential for embryonic development in part through the regulation of p53 pathway and controls the expansion growth of digestive organs and liver [[cite:PUB00097919], [cite:PUB00097921]]. UTP25 mediates, with CAPN3, the proteasome-independent degradation of p53/TP53 [[cite:PUB00097921], [cite:PUB00097922]]. These proteins display limited sequence similarity to DEAD-box RNA helicases, having alternative residues at the Walker A and DEAD-box sites, but conservation of structural and other key residues [[cite:PUB00109164]].

Members of this entry consist of two domains; this entry represents the bigger one, towards the N-terminal which is structurally related to NTPases, lacking the conserved motifs typically found in helicases (WalkerA/B motifs and motif Q). The C-terminal domain is represented in [interpro:IPR053939] and is required and sufficient for the interaction of UTP25 with Utp3. UTP25 interacts with nucleolar protein Nop19 in S. cerevisiae, and Nop19p is essential for the incorporation of Utp25p into pre-ribosomes [[cite:PUB00074620]].

Name: UTP25, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: UTP25 is a family of eukaryotic proteins. The family displays limited sequence similarity to DEAD-box RNA helicases, having alternative residues at the Walker A and DEAD-box sites, but conservation of structural and other key residues [[cite:PUB00109164]]. This entry represents the C-terminal domain that is required and sufficient for the interaction of Utp25 with Utp3. UTP25 interacts with nucleolar protein Nop19 in S. cerevisiae, and Nop19p is essential for the incorporation of Utp25p into pre-ribosomes [[cite:PUB00074620]]. Proteins in this entry consist of two domains; the C-terminal one is represented in this model.

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 25
ShortDescription:
This family represents U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 25 (UTP25), a DEAD-box RNA helicase-like protein component of the ribosomal small subunit processome for the biogenesis of ribosomes, which functions in pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) processing. U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 25 homologue (also known as Digestive organ expansion factor (DEF)) from animals is essential for embryonic development in part through the regulation of p53 pathway and controls the expansion growth of digestive organs and liver [[cite:PUB00097919], [cite:PUB00097921], [cite:PUB00097922]]. It is though to be also involved in the sympathetic neuronal development. UTP25 mediates, with CAPN3, the proteasome-independent degradation of p53/TP53 [[cite:PUB00097921], [cite:PUB00097922]].

Protein NUCLEOLAR FACTOR 1 from Arabidopsis thaliana (Nof1) is also included in this group. This protein is involved in the control of rRNA expression, embryo development and female gametogenesis [[cite:PUB00100328]].

Name: Ribosomal biogenesis protein FAF1-like
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in the maturation of ribosomes, which are essential cellular machines for protein synthesis. Members of this family are implicated in the processing of precursor ribosomal RNA (rRNA), specifically contributing to the cleavage events that are necessary for the proper formation of the 40S ribosomal subunit. The proteins in this family appear to play a role in the early stages of rRNA processing, participating in the cleavage at specific sites within the precursor rRNA molecule.

Name: Utp10/HEAT1, HEAT-repeats domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a HEAT-repeats domain found in HEATR1, Utp10 and similar eukaryotic proteins.

;

Proteins in this entry contain an armadillo-type fold, and a BP28, C-terminal domain. It includes HEAT repeat -containing protein 1 (HEATR1) from human and its orthologues from fungi, U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10 (Utp10), which is a HEAT-repeat containing protein involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]]. Utp10 is also involved in 40S ribosome maturation [[cite:PUB00090010]]. HEATR1 is a ribosome biogenesis factor required for recruitment of Myc to nucleoli [[cite:PUB00158858], [cite:PUB00151110]]. It is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and it is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00090011]]. HEATR1 plays a role in neuronal-lineage cell proliferation [[cite:PUB00158858]].

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10
ShortDescription: Proteins in this entry contain an armadillo-type fold, and a BP28, C-terminal domain. It includes HEAT repeat -containing protein 1 (HEATR1) from human and its orthologues from fungi, U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10 (Utp10), which is a HEAT-repeat containing protein involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]]. Utp10 is also involved in 40S ribosome maturation [[cite:PUB00090010]]. HEATR1 is a ribosome biogenesis factor required for recruitment of Myc to nucleoli [[cite:PUB00158858], [cite:PUB00151110]]. It is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and it is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00090011]]. HEATR1 plays a role in neuronal-lineage cell proliferation [[cite:PUB00158858]].

Name: BP28, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in the C-terminal of BAP28 proteins [[cite:PUB00016366]] (which are involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and ribosome biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00043646]]) and in other BAP28-like proteins.

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 10, N-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents the N-terminal domain of Utp10, which is a HEAT-repeat containing protein involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]]. Utp10 is also involved in 40S ribosome maturation [[cite:PUB00090010]]. Proteins containing this domain also include HEATR1 from humans. HEATR1 is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00090011]].

Name: DDX52/Rok1, DEAD-box helicase domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the DEAD-box helicase domain found in DDX52 from animals and Rok1 from yeasts. This domain contains the ATP-binding region. Rok1 is an RNA helicase involved in pre-rRNA processing and in control of cell cycle progression [[cite:PUB00097023]]. In humans, DDX52 is ubiquitously expressed in testis, endometrium, and other tissues [[cite:PUB00054674]]. DDX52 from Drosophila has been identified as part of a translational control module, also containing pths/DDX47 and ath/DHX33, which coordinates germline stem cell differentiation with ribosome biogenesis during oogenesis. This module allows for coregulation of ribosomal proteins and non1/GTPBP4, a p53 repressor, preventing p53 stabilization, cell cycle arrest and loss of stem cell differentiation [[cite:PUB00101919]].

Name: Exosome RNA helicase MTR4-like, stalk
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the helical stalk found at the N-terminal of KOW β-barrel from MTR4 [[cite:PUB00058447], [cite:PUB00057873], [cite:PUB00129868]]. This entry also includes Ski2-like helicases which have an overall similar structure to MTR4 proteins. However, Ski2 from yeast does not have the KOW motif and the β-barrel is tightly packed against the helical stalk [[cite:PUB00058447]].

;

Exosome RNA helicase Mtr4 is a essential RNA helicase, and is an exosome-activating cofactor. It functions together with the nuclear exosome being involved in processing of structured RNAs, including snRNAs and snoRNAs. It also plays a role in nuclear RNA surveillance pathways involving the so-called TRAMP complex [[cite:PUB00057873], [cite:PUB00129868], [cite:PUB00151589]]. It contains an arch domain, required for proper 5.8S rRNA processing, and appears to function independently of canonical helicase activity [[cite:PUB00151589]]. The arch domain comprises an helical stalk/elbow that flanks a KOW module which adopts a β-barrel fold [[cite:PUB00058447]].

Name: ATP-dependent RNA helicase Ski2/MTR4, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This C-terminal domain is found in Ski2/MTR4/helY-like DEAD box helicases [[cite:PUB00016366], [cite:PUB00058447]].

Name: Prismane-like superfamily
ShortDescription:
Prismane (hybrid-cluster) proteins are present in a wide range of bacteria and archaea, and are characterised by their two Fe/S centres: a [4Fe-4S] cubane cluster, and a hybrid [4Fe-2S-2O] cluster [[cite:PUB00007375]]. Prismane proteins contain four domains: two spectrin repeat-like 3-helical bundle domains, and two α/β domains with Rossmann-fold topology. Several proteins are structurally related to Prismane, including Ni-containing carbon monoxide dehydrogenase (CODH) (lack one of the N-terminal 3-helical bundle domains), the alpha and beta subunits of bifunctional CODH, and the alpha and beta subunits of acetyl-CoA synthetase.

This superfamily represents the spectrin repeat-like 3-helical bundle domains, as well as the two α/β domains with Rossmann-fold topology.

Name: Exosome RNA helicase MTR4-like, beta-barrel domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the β-barrel of MTR4 and related Ski2-like helicases. Ski2 from yeast has an overall similar structure to MTR4 proteins. However, it does not have the KOW motif [[cite:PUB00058447]] and it is not included in this entry. This entry also includes Circadian oscillator component FRH.

;

It functions together with the nuclear exosome being involved in processing of structured RNAs, including snRNAs and snoRNAs. It also plays a role in nuclear RNA surveillance pathways involving the so-called TRAMP complex [[cite:PUB00057873], [cite:PUB00129868], [cite:PUB00151589]]. It contains an arch domain, required for proper 5.8S rRNA processing, and appears to function independently of canonical helicase activity [[cite:PUB00151589]]. The arch domain comprises an helical stalk/elbow that flanks a KOW module which adopts a β-barrel fold [[cite:PUB00058447]].

Name: Circadian oscillator component FRH-like
ShortDescription:
This family represents a group of ATP-dependent RNA helicases and their homologues, including Circadian oscillator component FRH (FRH), Superkiller complex protein 2 (SKI2) and RNA helicase Mtr4 (also known as Dob1). This entry also includes DExH-box ATP-dependent RNA helicase DExH9 from Arabidopsis thaliana which target specific subsets of nuclear transcripts for degradation by the nuclear exosome [[cite:PUB00074527]].

;

FRH is a core component of the circadian oscillator, forming the FRC complex together with FRQ proteins [[cite:PUB00163261]]. This complex functions as the negative arm of the oscillator, inhibiting the activity of the WCC complex (composed of WC1 and WC2), thereby establishing the negative feedback loop that drives circadian rhythms [[cite:PUB00163261]]. The circadian clock governs the rhythmic expression of transcription factors, such as ZAFA and CZF1, which are vital for fungal adaptation to zinc starvation stress and the production of secondary metabolites [[cite:PUB00163261]]. In Fusarium oxysporum, the circadian clock controls pathogenesis in tomato plants, with infections causing the most severe disease symptoms at dawn [[cite:PUB00163261]].

;

SKI2 is a RNA helicase that forms Ski complex, which participates in many cytoplasmic pathways of the exosome in both yeast and metazoan cells, including 3'-to-5' mRNA turnover [[cite:PUB00074525], [cite:PUB00151108], [cite:PUB00151109]].

;

Mtr4 is a ATP-dependent 3'-5' RNA helicase involved in nuclear RNA processing and degradation [[cite:PUB00074526], [cite:PUB00074528]].

Name: ATP-dependent RNA helicase SUPV3-like
ShortDescription:
This entry represents ATP-dependent RNA helicase SUPV3L1, mitochondrial and related ATP-dependent RNA helicases found in bacteria and eukaryotes including Probable helicase HelY from bacteria.

;

SUPV3L1 is a major helicase involved in mitochondrial RNA metabolism. It is a component of the mitochondrial degradosome (mtEXO) complex, which degrades 3' overhang double-stranded RNA with 3'-to-5' directionality in an ATP-dependent manner [[cite:PUB00095346]]. SUPV3L1 functions as an ATPase and ATP-dependent multisubstrate helicase, capable of unwinding double-stranded DNA, double-stranded RNA, and RNA/DNA heteroduplexes in the 5'-to-3' direction. The protein plays a central role in the mitochondrial RNA surveillance system, regulating the stability of mature mRNAs, removing aberrantly formed mRNAs, and rapidly degrading non-coding processing intermediates, including non-coding mitochondrial transcripts (MT-ncRNA) and tRNA-like molecules [[cite:PUB00095346]]. SUPV3L1 is also implicated in recombination and chromatin maintenance pathways, associates with mitochondrial DNA, and may protect cells from apoptosis.

Name: U3 small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex, subunit Mpp10
ShortDescription: Mpp10 (M phase phosphoprotein 10) is a component of the 60-80S U3 small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (U3 snoRNP) required for three cleavage events that generate the mature 18S rRNA from the pre-rRNA [[cite:PUB00009804], [cite:PUB00019879]].

Name: Nucleolar protein 10-like, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found at the N-terminal of human Nucleolar protein 10 (NOL10) and similar eukaryotic sequences including the orthologue from yeast Ribosome biogenesis protein (ENP2). This domain is normally found N-terminal to [interpro:IPR056550]. This entry includes a entire β-propeller structure and two α-helices.

;

NOL10 (also known as Polyglutamine binding protein 5 (PQBP5)) binds to polyglutamine tract sequences and is expressed in the nucleolus. It makes up the skeletal structure of the nucleolus, constituting the granule meshwork in the granular component area, and functions as an anchor for reassembly of other nucleolar proteins [[cite:PUB00158898]].

ENP2 was identified in a set of proteins involved in rRNA-processing and ribosome biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00075792]].

Name: Nucleolar protein 10-like, second domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found in human Nucleolar protein 10 (NOL10) and similar eukaryotic sequences including the orthologue from yeast, Ribosome biogenesis protein (ENP2). This domain is normally found N-terminal to [interpro:IPR012580]. It is predicted to adopt an α-β configuration.

Name: Nucleolar protein 10/Enp2
ShortDescription: Proteins in this entry contain WD40 repeats. Nucleolar protein 10 (NOL10) is found in the nucleolus of vertebrates and contains seven WD40 repeats but is otherwise uncharacterised. Ribosome biogenesis protein Enp2 (Enp2) from Saccharomyces cerevisiae contains five WD40 repeats and is a component of 90S pre-ribosomes [[cite:PUB00090885]]. Homologues are also known from plants.

Name: AT hook, DNA-binding motif
ShortDescription: AT hooks are DNA-binding motifs with a preference for A/T rich regions. These motifs are found in a variety of proteins, including the high mobility group (HMG) proteins [[cite:PUB00044075]], in DNA-binding proteins from plants [[cite:PUB00044076]] and in hBRG1 protein, a central ATPase of the human switching/sucrose non-fermenting (SWI/SNF) remodelling complex [[cite:PUB00044077]].

Name: High mobility group protein HMGA
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the HMGA family, whose members contain DNA-binding domains, also known as AT hooks due to their ability to interact with the narrow minor groove of AT-rich DNA sequences. They play an important role in chromatin organisation [[cite:PUB00074434]].

;

The high mobility group (HMG) proteins are the most abundant and ubiquitous nonhistone chromosomal proteins. They bind to DNA and to nucleosomes and are involved in the regulation of DNA-dependent processes such as transcription, replication, recombination, and DNA repair. They can be grouped into three families: HMGB (HMG 1/2), HMGN (HMG 14/17) and HMGA (HMG I/Y). The characteristic domains are: AT-hook for the HMGA family, the HMG Box for the HMGB family, and the nucleosome-binding domain (NBD) for the members of the HMGN family [[cite:PUB00074432]].

ShortDescription:

In the mouse, Nrap is ubiquitously expressed and is specifically localised in the nucleolus. Nrap is a large nucleolar protein (of more than 1000 amino acids). Nrap appears to be associated with ribosome biogenesis by interacting with pre-rRNA primary transcript [[cite:PUB00008443]].

Name: Utp8, beta-propeller
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal β-propeller of U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 8 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Utp8) and similar proteins mainly found in ascomycetes. Utp8 is an essential component of the nuclear tRNA export machinery in S. cerevisiae. It is a tRNA-binding protein that acts at a step between tRNA maturation /aminoacylation, and translocation of the tRNA across the nuclear pore complex [[cite:PUB00044528]]. It is also co-purified with the U3 snoRNA containing complex, the small subunit (SSU) processome, which is required for the biogenesis of the 18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00008496]].

This entry also include the C1565.05 protein from Schizosaccharomyces pombe. Its function is not clear.

Name: Utp8, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This domain is found at the C-terminal of U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 8 (Utp8) from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and similar proteins from fungi. Utp8 is an essential component of the nuclear tRNA export machinery in S. cerevisiae. It is a tRNA binding protein that acts at a step between tRNA maturation /aminoacylation, and translocation of the tRNA across the nuclear pore complex [[cite:PUB00044528]]. It is also co-purified with the U3 snoRNA containing complex, the small subunit (SSU) processome, which is required for the biogenesis of the 18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00008496]]. This entry also includes the C1565.05 protein from Schizosaccharomyces pombe. Its function is not clear. This domain shows an all-α structure.

Name: Nucleotide-binding alpha-beta plait domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents nucleotide-binding domains with an α-β plait structure, which consists of either a ferredoxin-like (β-α-β)2 fold, such as that found in RNA-binding domains of various ribonucleoproteins or in viral DNA-binding domains [[cite:PUB00016352], [cite:PUB00007413]]; or a β-(α)-β-α-β(2) fold, such as that found in the ribosomal protein L23 [[cite:PUB00016354]].

Name: RNA-binding domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Many eukaryotic proteins containing one or more copies of a putative RNA-binding domain of about 90 amino acids are known to bind single-stranded RNAs [[cite:PUB00005341], [cite:PUB00034493], [cite:PUB00034494]]. The largest group of single strand RNA-binding proteins is the eukaryotic RNA recognition motif (RRM) family that contains an eight amino acid RNP-1 consensus sequence [[cite:PUB00001891], [cite:PUB00034495]]. RRM proteins have a variety of RNA binding preferences and functions, and include heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs), proteins implicated in regulation of alternative splicing (SR, U2AF, Sxl), protein components of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (U1 and U2 snRNPs), and proteins that regulate RNA stability and translation (PABP, La, Hu) [[cite:PUB00034493], [cite:PUB00034494], [cite:PUB00034495]]. The RRM in heterodimeric splicing factor U2 snRNP auxiliary factor (U2AF) appears to have two RRM-like domains with specialised features for protein recognition [[cite:PUB00016352]]. The motif also appears in a few single stranded DNA binding proteins.

The typical RRM consists of four anti-parallel β-strands and two α-helices arranged in a β-α-β-β-α-β fold with side chains that stack with RNA bases. Specificity of RNA binding is determined by multiple contacts with surrounding amino acids. A third helix is present during RNA binding in some cases [[cite:PUB00004440]]. The RRM is reviewed in a number of publications [[cite:PUB00034496], [cite:PUB00034497], [cite:PUB00034498]].

This entry also includes some bacterial putative RNA-binding proteins.

Name: ABT1/ESF2, RNA recognition motif
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the RNA recognition motif (RRM) of a novel nuclear protein termed ABT1 and its homologous counterpart, pre-rRNA-processing protein Esf2 (eighteen S factor 2), from yeast.

ABT1 associates with the TATA-binding protein (TBP) and enhances basal transcription activity of class II promoters. Meanwhile, ABT1 could be a transcription cofactor that can bind to DNA in a sequence-independent manner [[cite:PUB00083327]].

Name: ABT1/Esf2
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the nuclear protein ABT1 and its homologous counterpart, pre-rRNA-processing protein Esf2 (eighteen S factor 2), from yeast.

ABT1 associates with the TATA-binding protein (TBP) and enhances basal transcription activity of class II promoters. Meanwhile, ABT1 could be a transcription cofactor that can bind to DNA in a sequence-independent manner [[cite:PUB00083327]].

Name: Exosome complex component Csl4
ShortDescription:
This entry includes archaeal exosome complex component Csl4 and its homologues from eukaryotes (also known as exosome component 1 EXOSC1 in mammals). In budding yeast, Csl4 is also known as Ski4 due to its superkiller (SKI) phenotype first described as a more efficient ability to kill sensitive non-killer yeast strains [[cite:PUB00090086], [cite:PUB00090084]]. Later, it was found to be part of the yeast exosome complex involved in 3'-5' RNA processing and degradation in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm [[cite:PUB00090085]].

;

Csl4 is a non-catalytic component of the exosome, a complex involved in RNA processing and degradation [[cite:PUB00035570], [cite:PUB00074124]]. The exact composition of the exosome varies, depending on the organism or the subcellular localization, but in all cases it is composed of a ring-shaped core made of three heterodimers (Rrp41p/Rrp45p, Rrp43p /Rrp46p, Rrp42p/Mtr3p) stabilized by the presence of three other proteins (Csl4/Ski4, Rrp4p, Rrp40p) [[cite:PUB00090084]]. The presence of different proteins in the cap may enable interactions with different substrates. It has been shown that the archaeal DnaG protein needs Csl4 for binding to the exosome. DnaG is a poly(A)-binding protein and enhances the degradation of adenine-rich transcripts by the Csl4-exosome [[cite:PUB00074085]].

Name: Exosome complex component CSL4, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found at the N-terminal of Exosome complex component CSL4 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a non-catalytic component of the RNA exosome complex which has 3'->5' exoribonuclease activity and participates in a multitude of cellular RNA processing and degradation events [[cite:PUB00065825], [cite:PUB00152001], [cite:PUB00151981], [cite:PUB00152002]].

Name: Exosome complex component CSL4, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
Exosome is a complex of 3' --> 5' exoribonucleases that play a major role in diverse RNA processing and degradation pathways. The eukaryotic exosome complex contains 9 proteins. Six RNase PH domain containing proteins (Rrp41, Rrp42, Rrp43, Rrp45, Rrp46, and Mtr3) form a catalytic ring, three RNA binding domain containing proteins (Rrp4,Rrp40, and Csl4) bind on top of the ring [[cite:PUB00035569]].

This entry represents the C-terminal domain of the exosome complex component CSL4 (also known as EXOSC1). CSL4 does not have exonuclease activity, but are required for the 3'-processing of the 7S pre-RNA to the mature 5.8S rRNA and for mRNA decay [[cite:PUB00045433], [cite:PUB00045434]].

Name: Possible tRNA binding domain
ShortDescription: This domain, found at the C terminus of tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase, may be involved in tRNA-binding [[cite:PUB00050413]]. tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase TmcA catalyses the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine (ac4C) at the wobble position of tRNA(Met), by using acetyl-CoA as an acetyl donor and ATP (or GTP) [[cite:PUB00056806]].

Name: RNA cytidine acetyltransferase NAT10
ShortDescription:
RNA cytidine acetyltransferase NAT10 has specificity toward both 18S rRNA and tRNAs and catalyzes the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine at two positions in 18S rRNA. NAT10 is required for early nucleolar cleavages of precursor rRNA at sites A0, A1 and A2 during 18S rRNA synthesis [[cite:PUB00077545], [cite:PUB00076725]]. NAT10 also catalyzes the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine at a single position in serine and leucine tRNAs. The tRNA-binding adapter protein TAN1 is required for full tRNA acetyltransferase activity but not for 18S rRNA acetylation [[cite:PUB00076725]].

Human NAT10 is a lysine acetyltransferase that targets microtubules and histones, and plays an important role in cell division. It is highly expressed in malignant tumors [[cite:PUB00080263]].

Name: TmcA/NAT10, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain found at the N-terminal of TmcA from bacteria and NAT10 from eukaryotes.

;

The bacterial tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase (TmcA) catalyses the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine (ac4C) at the wobble position of tRNA(Met), by using acetyl-CoA as an acetyl donor and either ATP or GTP [[cite:PUB00056806]]. This modification is thought to ensure precise recognition of the AUG codon by strengthening C-G base-pair interaction and also prevent misrecognition of the near cognate AUA codon [[cite:PUB00050413]]. RNA cytidine acetyltransferas (NAT10) are RNA cytosine acetyltransferases with specificity toward both 18S rRNA and tRNAs and contain additional putative nuclear and nucleolar localisation signals (NLS and NoLS respectively) [[cite:PUB00076725], [cite:PUB00076726], [cite:PUB00107449]].

Name: TmcA/NAT10/Kre33
ShortDescription:
This entry includes bacterial tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase TmcA and eukaryotic N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10). They consist of an RNA helicase domain and a GCN5-related N-acetyltransferase (GNAT) domain.

Name: TcmA/NAT10, helicase domain
ShortDescription:
This domain contains a P-loop (Walker A) motif, suggesting that it has ATPase activity, and a Walker B motif. It is found in NAT10 from eukaryotes and TmcA from prokaryotes. In NAT10, this domain catalyses the formation of N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modification on mRNAs, 18S rRNA and tRNAs [[cite:PUB00076725], [cite:PUB00158942], [cite:PUB00158943]]. In TmcA, it may function as an RNA helicase motor (driven by ATP hydrolysis) which delivers the wobble base to the active centre of the GCN5-related N-acetyltransferase (GNAT) domain [[cite:PUB00050413]].

Name: Brix domain
ShortDescription:
Analysis of the Brix (biogenesis of ribosomes in Xenopus) protein leaded to the identification of a region of 150-180 residues length, called the Brix domain, which is found in six protein families: one archaean family (I) including hypothetical proteins (one per genome); and five eukaryote families, each named according to a representative member and including close homologues of this prototype: (II) Peter Pan (D. melanogaster) and SSF1/2 (S.cerevisiae); (III) RPF1 (S. cerevisiae); (IV) IMP4 (S. cerevisiae); (V) Brix (X.laevis) and BRX1 (S. cerevisiae); and (VI) RPF2 (S.cerevisiae).

Typically, a protein sequence belonging to the Brix domain superfamily contains a highly charged N-terminal segment (about 50 residues) followed by a single copy of the Brix domain and another highly charged C-terminal region (about 100 residues). The archaean sequences have two unique characteristics: (1) the charged regions are totally absent at the N terminus and are reduced in number to about 10 residues at the C terminus; and (2) the C-terminal part of the Brix domain itself is minimal. Two eukaryote groups have large insertions within the C-terminal region: about 70 residues in the group III and about 120 in the group II. Biological data for some proteins in this family suggest a role in ribosome biogenesis and rRNA binding [[cite:PUB00018304], [cite:PUB00018305], [cite:PUB00095726], [cite:PUB00060567]].

Name: U3 snoRNP protein/Ribosome production factor 1
ShortDescription: This family represents the U3 small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein protein IMP4 and Ribosome production factor 1 RPF1 that belong to the IMP4 superfamily. This superfamily contains a Brix (biogenesis of ribosomes in Xenopus) domain, a region of 150-180 residues length, and it is characterised by the sigma70-like motif, a sequence motif first identified in the sigma70 family of prokaryotic transcription factors, which is sufficient to confer RNA binding activity [[cite:PUB00095723], [cite:PUB00019232], [cite:PUB00060567]]. IMP4 is a component of the 60-80S U3 small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (U3 snoRNP) and it is required for the early cleavages during pre-18S ribosomal RNA processing [[cite:PUB00095723], [cite:PUB00095726]]. RPF1 is a essential protein involved in ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00019232]].

Name: Actin, conserved site
ShortDescription:
Actin [[cite:PUB00000090], [cite:PUB00001058]] is a ubiquitous protein involved in the formation of filaments that are major components of the cytoskeleton. These filaments interact with myosin to produce a sliding effect, which is the basis of muscular contraction and many aspects of cell motility, including cytokinesis. Each actin protomer binds one molecule of ATP and has one high affinity site for either calcium or magnesium ions, as well as several low affinity sites. Actin exists as a monomer in low salt concentrations, but filaments form rapidly as salt concentration rises, with the consequent hydrolysis of ATP. Actin from many sources forms a tight complex with deoxyribonuclease (DNase I) although the significance of this is still unknown. The formation of this complex results in the inhibition of DNase I activity, and actin loses its ability to polymerise. It has been shown that an ATPase domain of actin shares similarity with ATPase domains of hexokinase and hsp70 proteins [[cite:PUB00004744], [cite:PUB00004796]].

In vertebrates there are three groups of actin isoforms: alpha, beta and gamma. The alpha actins are found in muscle tissues and are a major constituent of the contractile apparatus. The beta and gamma actins co-exists in most cell types as components of the cytoskeleton and as mediators of internal cell motility. In plants there are many isoforms which are probably involved in a variety of functions such as cytoplasmic streaming, cell shape determination, tip growth, graviperception, cell wall deposition, etc.

This entry contains a signature that picks up both actins and the actin-like proteins and corresponds to positions 106 to 118 in actins.

Name: Actin family
ShortDescription:
Actin [[cite:PUB00000090], [cite:PUB00001058]] is a ubiquitous protein involved in the formation of filaments that are major components of the cytoskeleton. These filaments interact with myosin to produce a sliding effect, which is the basis of muscular contraction and many aspects of cell motility, including cytokinesis. Each actin protomer binds one molecule of ATP and has one high affinity site for either calcium or magnesium ions, as well as several low affinity sites. Actin exists as a monomer in low salt concentrations, but filaments form rapidly as salt concentration rises, with the consequent hydrolysis of ATP. Actin from many sources forms a tight complex with deoxyribonuclease (DNase I) although the significance of this is still unknown. The formation of this complex results in the inhibition of DNase I activity, and actin loses its ability to polymerise. It has been shown that an ATPase domain of actin shares similarity with ATPase domains of hexokinase and hsp70 proteins [[cite:PUB00004744], [cite:PUB00004796]].

In vertebrates there are three groups of actin isoforms: alpha, beta and gamma. The alpha actins are found in muscle tissues and are a major constituent of the contractile apparatus. The beta and gamma actins co-exists in most cell types as components of the cytoskeleton and as mediators of internal cell motility. In plants there are many isoforms which are probably involved in a variety of functions such as cytoplasmic streaming, cell shape determination, tip growth, graviperception, cell wall deposition, etc.

Recently some divergent actin-like proteins have been identified in several species. These proteins include centractin (actin-RPV) from mammals, fungi yeast ACT5, Neurospora crassa ro-4 and Pneumocystis carinii, which seems to be a component of a multi-subunit centrosomal complex involved in microtubule based vesicle motility (this subfamily is known as ARP1); ARP2 subfamily, which includes chicken ACTL, Saccharomyces cerevisiae ACT2, Drosophila melanogaster 14D and Caenorhabditis elegans actC; ARP3 subfamily, which includes actin 2 from mammals, Drosophila 66B, yeast ACT4 and Schizosaccharomyces pombe act2; and ARP4 subfamily, which includes yeast ACT3 and Drosophila 13E.

Name: Core Histone H2A/H2B/H3 domain
ShortDescription:
Five major families of histones exist: H1/H5, H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 [[cite:PUB00066796]]. Histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 are known as the core histones, while histones H1 and H5 are known as the linker histones. The core histones together with some other DNA binding proteins form a superfamily defined by a common fold and distant sequence similarities [[cite:PUB00005743], [cite:PUB00005777]]. Some proteins contain local homology domains related to the histone fold [[cite:PUB00004260]].

This entry represents a domain found in histones H2A, H2B and H3. This domain can also be found in transcription factors, such as OsNF-YC2 from rice [[cite:PUB00094278]].

Name: Histone-fold
ShortDescription: Histones mediate DNA organisation and play a dominant role in regulating eukaryotic transcription. The histone-fold consists of a core of three helices, where the long middle helix is flanked at each end by shorter ones. The histone fold is a structural element that facilitates heterodimerisation [[cite:PUB00060941], [cite:PUB00060942], [cite:PUB00039806]]. Proteins displaying this structure include the nucleosome core histones, which form octomers composed of two copies of each of the four histones, H2A, H2B, H3 and H4; archaeal histone, which possesses only the core domain part of eukaryotic histone; and the TATA-box binding protein (TBP)-associated factors (TAF), where the histone fold is a common motif for mediating TAF-TAF interactions. TAF proteins include TAF(II)18 and TAF(II)28, which form a heterodimer, TAF(II)42 and TAF(II)62, which form a heterotetramer similar to (H3-H4)2, and the negative cofactor 2 (NC2) alpha and beta chains, which form a heterodimer. The TAF proteins are a component of transcription factor IID (TFIID), along with the TBP protein. TFIID forms part of the pre-initiation complex on core promoter elements required for RNA polymerase II-dependent transcription. The TAF subunits of TFIID mediate transcriptional activation of subsets of eukaryotic genes. The NC2 complex mediates the inhibition of TATA-dependent transcription through interactions with TBP.

Name: Histone H3/CENP-A
ShortDescription:
This entry includes histone H3 and its variant, CENP-A (Cse4 in budding yeast, Cnp1 in fission yeast, and CID/CenH3 in fruit flies). Two primate-specific forms of H3, known as H3.X and H3.Y, are found in the brain [[cite:PUB00090177]].

Histone H3 is one of the five histones, along with H1/H5, H2A, H2B and H4. Two copies of each of the H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 histones ensemble to form the core of the nucleosome [[cite:PUB00066796]]. The nucleosome forms octameric structure that wraps DNA in a left-handed manner. H3 is a highly conserved protein of 135 amino acid residues [[cite:PUB00004448], [cite:PUB00004388]]. Histones can undergo several different types of post-translational modifications that affect transcription, DNA repair, DNA replication and chromosomal stability.

Eukaryotic centromeres consists of an unique nucleosome in which CENP-A can be found [[cite:PUB00070934]]. Human CENP-A nucleosome forms a histone octamer containing two each of histones H2A, H2B, H4 and CENP-A. Similar to the H3-containing nucleosome, the CENP-A nucleosome wraps DNA in a left-handed orientation [[cite:PUB00070935], [cite:PUB00070936]]. CENP-A nucleosomes function as a scaffold on which other kinetochore proteins assemble. CENP-A may serves as an epigenetic marker for kinetochore assembly [[cite:PUB00070937]]. Deposition of CENP-A to the centromere requires histone chaperone HJURP (Holliday junction recognition protein) [[cite:PUB00070938]].

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 6, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal segment of UTP6 proteins. This region contains repeats related to TPR superfamily repeats [interpro:IPR011990].

;

Utp6 is a component of the small subunit (SSU) processome containing the U3 snoRNA that is involved in processing of pre-18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00008496]].

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 6
ShortDescription: Utp6 is a component of the small subunit (SSU) processome containing the U3 snoRNA that is involved in processing of pre-18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00008496]].

Name: Peptidase S9, N-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents the β-propeller domain found at the N-terminal of prolyl oligopeptidases, including acylamino-acid-releasing enzyme (also known as acylaminoacyl peptidase). The prolyl oligopeptidase family consist of a number of evolutionary related peptidases whose catalytic activity seems to be provided by a charge relay system similar to that of the trypsin family of serine proteases, but which evolved by independent convergent evolution. The N-terminal domain of prolyl oligopeptidases form an unusual 7-bladed β-propeller [[cite:PUB00020062], [cite:PUB00068074]].

Name: WD repeat-containing protein 75
ShortDescription: This entry includes WD repeat-containing protein 75 (WDR75) from animals and its orthologues, Nan1/Utp17 (NET1-associated nuclear protein 1) from yeast. These proteins are involved in ribosome biogenesis, specifically as factors within the small subunit (SSU) processome, which is the initial precursor to the small eukaryotic ribosomal subunit [[cite:PUB00151110], [cite:PUB00090011], [cite:PUB00008496], [cite:PUB00035837]]. These proteins are essential for various stages of pre-rRNA processing, including RNA folding, modification, rearrangement, and cleavage. They also contribute to the targeted degradation of pre-ribosomal RNA by the RNA exosome. Additionally, they play a crucial role in the nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA and are necessary for the optimal transcription of pre-ribosomal RNA by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00035837]].

Name: HECT domain
ShortDescription: The HECT (Homologous to the E6-AP Carboxyl Terminus) domain is an around 350 amino acids motif that has been identified in proteins that all belong to a particular E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase family [[cite:PUB00004858]]. HECT domain containing proteins accept ubiquitin from an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme in the form of a thioester and then transfer it to lysine side chains of target proteins, and transfers additional ubiquitin molecules to the end of growing ubiquitin chains. The site of ubiquitin thioester formation is a conserved cysteine residue located in the last 32-36 aa of the HECT domain [[cite:PUB00004858]]. The amino-terminal part of the HECT domain has been involved in E2 binding [[cite:PUB00018224], [cite:PUB00081573]]. Once linked to ubiquitin, the target proteins are degraded in the 26 S proteasome.

Name: E3 ubiquitin ligase, domain of unknown function DUF908
ShortDescription: This is a domain of unknown function found at the N terminus of a family of E3 ubiquitin protein ligases, including yeast TOM1, many of which appear to play a role in mRNA transcription and processing. This domain is found in association with and immediately N-terminal to another domain of unknown function: [interpro:IPR010314].

Name: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase
ShortDescription: The protein family described is involved in the ubiquitination process, where members act as E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases. These enzymes accept ubiquitin from E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes as thioesters and transfer them directly to target substrates. This post-translational modification can lead to various outcomes, including proteasomal degradation, altered cellular location, or changes in activity of the substrate proteins. The family members regulate diverse biological processes such as signal transduction, cell cycle progression, apoptosis, DNA repair, mRNA export, rRNA maturation, and immune responses. Some proteins within the family also have roles in regulating membrane dynamics, neuronal development, and autophagy. They are characterized by the presence of HECT, WW, or C2 domains, which mediate interactions with substrates and regulatory proteins, and are involved in autoinhibition and activation of the ligase activity.

Name: HECT, E3 ligase catalytic domain
ShortDescription: The HECT (Homologous to the E6-AP Carboxyl Terminus) domain is an around 350 amino acids motif that has been identified in proteins that all belong to a particular E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase family [[cite:PUB00004858]]. HECT domain containing proteins accept ubiquitin from an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme in the form of a thioester and then transfer it to lysine side chains of target proteins, and transfers additional ubiquitin molecules to the end of growing ubiquitin chains. The site of ubiquitin thioester formation is a conserved cysteine residue located in the last 32-36 aa of the HECT domain [[cite:PUB00004858]]. The amino-terminal part of the HECT domain has been involved in E2 binding [[cite:PUB00018224], [cite:PUB00081573]]. Once linked to ubiquitin, the target proteins are degraded in the 26 S proteasome.

Name: HUWE1/REV1, ubiquitin-binding motif
ShortDescription: This entry contains repetitive elements (RE) from a subgroup of HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases and the Y-family translesion polymerases, including human HUWE1 and REV1. Each of these repetitive elements are approximately 20 amino acids in length and contain two predicted helical segments separated by a Leu-Pro motif. The REs from the Y-family polymerases were shown to bind ubiquitin and were the basis for a novel ubiquitin-binding domain called the ubiquitin-binding motif (UBM) [[cite:PUB00091009], [cite:PUB00102678], [cite:PUB00103302]].

Name: E3 ubiquitin ligase, domain of unknown function DUF913
ShortDescription: This is a domain of unknown function found towards the N terminus of a family of E3 ubiquitin protein ligases, including yeast TOM1, many of which appear to play a role in mRNA transcription and processing. This domain is found in association with and immediately C-terminal to another domain of unknown function: [interpro:IPR010309].

Name: Oxidoreductase Oye-like
ShortDescription: This entry include a group of oxidoreductases, found in the Old yellow enzyme (OYE) family which includes 12-oxophytodienoate reductase, pentaerythritol tetranitrate reductase, morphinone reductase, and related enzymes. It includes Oye2/3 from budding yeasts. Oye2/3 are flavin-dependent NADPH oxidoreductases that have roles in oxidative stress and programmed cell death in yeast [[cite:PUB00098358]].

Name: Aldolase-type TIM barrel
ShortDescription: This entry represents the TIM β/α barrel found in aldolase and in related proteins. This TIM barrel usually covers the entire protein structure. Proteins containing this TIM barrel domain include class I aldolases, class I DAHP synthases, class II fructose-bisphosphate aldolases (FBP aldolases), and 5-aminolevulinate dehydratase (a hybrid of classes I and II aldolases) [[cite:PUB00027702], [cite:PUB00023436], [cite:PUB00027703]].

Name: NADH:flavin oxidoreductase/NADH oxidase, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
The TIM-barrel fold is a closed barrel structure composed of an eight-fold repeat of β-α units, where the eight parallel β strands on the inside are covered by the eight α helices on the outside [[cite:PUB00027645]]. It is a widely distributed fold which has been found in many enzyme families that catalyse completely unrelated reactions [[cite:PUB00027646]]. The active site is always found at the C-terminal end of this domain.

Proteins in this entry are a variety of NADH:flavin oxidoreductase/NADH oxidase enzymes, found mostly in bacteria or fungi, that contain a TIM-barrel fold. They commonly use FMN/FAD as cofactor and include:

  • dimethylamine dehydrogenase
  • trimethylamine dehydrogenase
  • 12-oxophytodienoate reductase
  • NADPH dehydrogenase
  • NADH oxidase

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated WD repeat-containing protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in ribosome biogenesis, particularly in the processing and transcription of pre-18S ribosomal RNA. Members of this family are part of the small subunit (SSU) processome, which is the first precursor of the small eukaryotic ribosomal subunit. They play a role in coordinating the assembly of ribosome biogenesis factors, RNA chaperones, and ribosomal proteins with nascent pre-rRNA to facilitate RNA folding, modifications, rearrangements, and cleavage. Additionally, they are involved in the targeted degradation of pre-ribosomal RNA by the RNA exosome and are essential for maintaining high-level expression of target genes during transcription. These proteins are also required for stem cell pluripotency and embryonic development.

Name: DEAD-box helicase, OB fold
ShortDescription: This domain is found towards the C terminus of the DEAD-box helicases ([interpro:IPR011545]). In these helicases it is apparently always found in association with [interpro:IPR007502]. There do seem to be a couple of instances where it occurs by itself - e.g. [swissprot:F4I9Q5]. This C-terminal domain of the yeast helicase contains an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-binding (OB)-fold which seems to be placed at the entrance of the putative nucleic acid cavity. It also constitutes the binding site for the G-patch-containing domain of Pfa1p. When found on DEAH/RHA helicases, this domain is central to the regulation of the helicase activity through its binding of both RNA and G-patch domain proteins [[cite:PUB00092307], [cite:PUB00064170]].

Name: Helicase-associated domain
ShortDescription: This is the helicase associated domain (HA2) found as a diverse set of RNA helicases. It has an all α-helical fold that can be divided in two subdomains, an N-terminal degenerated winged helix (WH) and a C-terminal ratchet-like domain [[cite:PUB00100845], [cite:PUB00100846], [cite:PUB00100848], [cite:PUB00100847]]. This domain collaborates with the RecA domains at the N-terminal in the formation of a RNA binding channel to allow the helicases to keep a stable grip on the RNA.

Name: DNA/RNA helicase, ATP-dependent, DEAH-box type, conserved site
ShortDescription:
A number of eukaryotic and prokaryotic proteins have been characterised [[cite:PUB00003826], [cite:PUB00004037], [cite:PUB00004089]] on the basis of their structural similarity. They all seem to be involved in ATP-dependent, nucleic-acid unwinding. There are two subfamilies of such proteins, the D-E-A-D-box and D-E-A-H-box families. Proteins that belong to the subfamily which have His instead of the second Asp are said to be 'D-E-A-H-box' proteins [[cite:PUB00004089], [cite:PUB00004395], [cite:PUB00003151]].

Proteins currently known to belong to this subfamily include yeast PRP2, PRP16, PRP22 and PRP43, involved in various ATP-requiring steps of the pre-mRNA splicing process; fission yeast prh1, which my be involved in pre-mRNA splicing; Drosophila male-less (mle) protein required in males for dosage compensation of X chromosome linked genes; yeast RAD3, a DNA helicase involved in excision repair of DNA damaged by UV light, bulky adducts or cross-linking agents; fission yeast rad15 (rhp3) and mammalian DNA excision repair protein XPD (ERCC-2); yeast CHL1 (or CTF1), which is important for chromosome transmission and normal cell cycle progression in G(2)/M; yeast TPS1, Caenorhabditis elegans hypothetical proteins C06E1.10 and K03H1.2; Poxviruses' early transcription factor 70kDa subunit which acts with RNA polymerase to initiate transcription from early gene promoters; Vaccinia virus putative helicase I8; and Escherichia coli putative RNA helicase hrpA. All these proteins share a number of conserved sequence motifs. Some of them are specific to this family while others are shared by other ATP-binding proteins or by proteins belonging to the helicases 'superfamily' [[cite:PUB00004021]].

Name: Helicase associated domain (HA2), winged-helix domain
ShortDescription: The helicase associated domain (HA2) has an all α-helical fold and consists of a N-terminal winged-helix (WH) domain and a C-terminal degenerate helical-bundle domain, referred to as the ratchet-like domain [[cite:PUB00100845], [cite:PUB00100846], [cite:PUB00100847]]. These domains collaborate with RecA domains at the N-terminal in completing an RNA binding channel to allow the helicases to keep a stable grip on the RNA [[cite:PUB00100847]] and assure its correct function. This entry represents the WH domain, which connects the N- (RecA domains) and C-terminal domains (ratchet-like and OB-fold) of helicases.

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 15, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of the U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 15 (UTP15). This protein is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA, and is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I together with a subset of U3 proteins required for transcription (t-UTPs). UTP15 is a component of the ribosomal small subunit (SSU) processome, which is a large ribonucleoprotein (RNP) required for processing of precursors to the small subunit RNA, the 18S, of the ribosome [[cite:PUB00035836], [cite:PUB00035837]]. This domain is found C-terminal to the WD40 repeat ([interpro:IPR001680]). UTP15 associates with U3 snoRNA, which is ubiquitous in eukaryotes and is required for nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA [[cite:PUB00008496]].

Name: Small-subunit processome, Utp14
ShortDescription:
A large ribonuclear protein complex is required for the processing of the small-ribosomal-subunit rRNA -the small-subunit (SSU) processome [[cite:PUB00008496], [cite:PUB00035836]]. This preribosomal complex contains the U3 snoRNA and at least 40 proteins, which have the following properties:

  • They are nucleolar.
  • They are able to coimmunoprecipitate with the U3 snoRNA and Mpp10 (a protein specific to the SSU processome).
  • They are required for 18S rRNA biogenesis.

There appears to be a linkage between polymerase I transcription and the formation of the SSU processome; as some, but not all, of the SSU processome components are required for pre-rRNA transcription initiation. These SSU processome components have been termed t-Utps. They form a pre-complex with pre-18S rRNA in the absence of snoRNA U3 and other SSU processome components. It has been proposed that the t-Utp complex proteins are both rDNA and rRNA binding proteins that are involved in the initiation of pre18S rRNA transcription. Initially binding to rDNA then associating with the 5' end of the nascent pre18S rRNA. The t-Utpcomplex forms the nucleus around which the rest of the SSU processome components, including snoRNA U3, assemble [[cite:PUB00035837]]. From electron microscopy the SSU processome may correspond to the terminal knobs visualised at the 5' ends of nascent 18S rRNA.

This entry contains Utp14, a large ribonuclear protein associated with snoRNA U3 [[cite:PUB00008496]].

Name: rRNA biogenesis protein RRP5, S1 domain, first repeat
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the first S1 from both Homo sapiens Rrp5 (hs1) and S. cerevisiae (sc1).

Rrp5 has two distinct regions, an N-terminal region containing tandemly repeated S1 RNA-binding domains (12 S1 repeats in Saccharomyces cerevisiae Rrp5 and 14 S1 repeats in Homo sapiens Rrp5) and a C-terminal region containing tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs thought to be involved in protein-protein interactions. Mutational studies have shown that each region represents a specific functional domain. Deletions within the S1-containing region inhibit pre-rRNA processing at either site A3 or A2, whereas deletions within the TPR region confer an inability to support cleavage of A0-A2.

;

Rrp5 is involved in the biogenesis of rRNA. It is required for formation of both 18S and 5.8S rRNA in budding yeasts [[cite:PUB00098267]]. In humans, it is also known as NFBP, which is essential for the generation of 18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00098268]]. In Arabidopsis, it is essential for normal development of female gametophytes [[cite:PUB00098269]].

ShortDescription: Rrp5 is involved in the biogenesis of rRNA. It is required for formation of both 18S and 5.8S rRNA in budding yeasts [[cite:PUB00098267]]. Name: Fcf1/UTP23
ShortDescription: Utp23 share homology with PINc domain protein Fcf1. They are components of the small subunit processome (SSU) that are involved in rRNA-processing and ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00035397], [cite:PUB00067997]].

Name: rRNA-processing protein Fcf1, PIN domain
ShortDescription:
Fcf1 (also known as Utp24) is an essential protein involved in pre-rRNA processing and 40S ribosomal subunit assembly [[cite:PUB00035397]]. As a component of the small subunit (SSU) processome, Fcf1 is an essential nucleolar protein required for processing of the 18S pre-rRNA at sites A0-A2 [[cite:PUB00067997]].

The PIN (PilT N terminus) domain is a compact RNA-binding protein domain found in all domains of life. Typically, the PIN domain contains three or four conserved acidic residues (putative metal-binding, active site residues) [[cite:PUB00087075]]. The Fcf1 PIN domain has four of these putative active site residues and the Fcf1-Utp23 homologue PIN domain has three of them. Point mutation studies of the conserved acidic residues in the putative active site of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Fcf1 determined they were essential for pre-rRNA processing at sites A1 and A2, whereas the presence of the Fcf1 protein itself is also required for cleavage at site A0 [[cite:PUB00067997], [cite:PUB00035397]].

Name: Exosome complex component RRP45
ShortDescription:
Rrp45, also known as EXOSC9, is a core component of the RNA exosome complex which participates in a multitude of cellular RNA processing and degradation events [[cite:PUB00045433]].

;

The conserved core of the exosome complex, the major eukaryotic 3' --> 5' exonuclease, consists of nine subunits that form a ring similar to the phosphorolytic bacterial PNPase and archaeal exosome [[cite:PUB00045434], [cite:PUB00035569]]. The complex functions in the accurate processing of nuclear RNA precursors and in the degradation of RNAs in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm [[cite:PUB00077701]].

Name: R3H domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
The R3H domain superfamily is a conserved sequence motif found in proteins from a diverse range of organisms including eubacteria, green plants, fungi and various groups of metazoans, but not in archaea and Escherichia coli. The domain is named R3H because it contains an invariant arginine and a highly conserved histidine, that are separated by three residues. It also displays a conserved pattern of hydrophobic residues, prolines and glycines. It can be found alone, in association with AAA domain or with various DNA/RNA binding domains like DSRM, KH, G-patch, PHD, DEAD box, or RRM. The functions of these domains indicate that the R3H domain might be involved in polynucleotide-binding, including DNA, RNA and single-stranded DNA [[cite:PUB00005485]].

The 3D structure of the R3H domain has been solved. The fold presents a small motif, consisting of a three-stranded antiparallel β-sheet, against which two α-helices pack from one side. This fold is related to the structures of the YhhP protein and the C-terminal domain of the translational initiation factor IF3. Three conserved basic residues cluster on the same face of the R3H domain and could play a role in nucleic acid recognition. An extended hydrophobic area at a different site of the molecular surface could act as a protein-binding site [[cite:PUB00018517]].

Name: R3H domain-containing
ShortDescription: The R3H domain-containing protein family is involved in various cellular processes. Members of this family are implicated in the regulation of germline mitosis, karyosome formation, and the establishment of dorsoventral polarity in eggs and embryos. They play a role in the localization and translation of grk mRNA in oocytes and may influence germline mitosis by promoting cyclin E proteolysis via the SCF-ubiquitin-proteasome complex. Additionally, certain isoforms within this family may function as competitive inhibitors of calmodulin-dependent enzymes, such as calcineurin, particularly in neuronal contexts.

Name: WD repeat-containing protein 75, second beta-propeller
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the second β-propeller found in WD repeat-containing protein 75 (WDR75) from animals. The function of this domain is unknown. This domain is also found in U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 13 and 17 (UTP13 and UTP17), which are WDR75 orthologs from yeast.

;

WDR75 is an essential factor in the early stages of ribosome assembly. It is a component of the small subunit (SSU) processome, which is the first precursor of the eukaryotic small ribosomal subunit [[cite:PUB00155547]]. WDR75 has a crucial positive role in ribosome biogenesis and its malfunction activates p53, leading to cellular senescence [[cite:PUB00155547]]. WDR75 is required for pre-rRNA transcription, supporting the maintenance of physiological levels of RPA194, a key subunit of RNA polymerase I. Its depletion leads to reduced rRNA synthesis and destabilization of RPA194, but not RPA135, another RNA Pol I component [[cite:PUB00160558]]

Name: Proteasome activator superfamily
ShortDescription: The 20S proteasome is a multicatalytic complex that is responsible for the non-lysosomal degradation of intracellular proteins. The proteasome is composed of a catalytic core that is regulated by protein complexes, which bind to the ends of the cylindrical core structure. One of these regulatory complexes is the PA28 activator complex (also known as the 11S regulator, or REG), a ring-shaped hexameric structure that enhances the peptidase activity of the core enzyme. Three REG subunits have been isolated, REGalpha, REGbeta and REGgamma. REGalpha and REGbeta preferentially form a heteromeric complex with alternating alpha and beta subunits. The structure of the human REGalpha subunit reveals a heptameric barrel-shaped assembly containing a central channel [[cite:PUB00013234]]. The binding of REG is thought to create a pore through with substrates and products can pass.

Name: Proteasome activator PA28, C-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
The specificity of the 20S proteasome, which degrades many intracellular proteins, is regulated by protein complexes that bind to one or both ends of the cylindrical proteasome structure. Proteasome activator 28 (PA28), also known as 11S regulator or REG, is one of these complexes. PA28 binds to the 20S proteasome and stimulates peptidase activity in and ATP-independent manner.

Three PA28 subunits that have been identified, PA28alpha, PA28beta and PA28gamma (also known as the Ki antigen), which share extensive sequence similarity, apart from a highly variable internal segment [[cite:PUB00013234]]. PA28alpha and PA28beta form a ring shaped hexameric structure of alternating alpha and beta subunits. The catalytic properties of PA28alpha and PA28beta-activated proteosome are similar [[cite:PUB00033208], [cite:PUB00033209]].

This entry represents the C-terminal domain superfamily found in the proteasome activator 28 subunits.

Name: Pre-rRNA-processing protein Esf1
ShortDescription: Pre-rRNA-processing protein Esf1 is required for the biogenesis of 18S rRNA in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It has a role in early pre-rRNA processing because it associates with U3 and U14 snoRNAs but not the SSU processome [[cite:PUB00090055]]. Homologues are found in other fungi, animals and plants.

Name: ESF1, RRM domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in the yeast Pre-rRNA-processing protein ESF1 and related eukaryotic proteins. ESF1 is involved in the 18S rRNA synthesis and required for the early cleavages at sites A0, A1 and A2 [[cite:PUB00090055]]. This domain has a detectable similarity to known RNA binding domains.

Name: Ribosomal RNA-processing protein Rrp9-like
ShortDescription: This entry includes Rrp9 from budding yeasts and its homologue, U3 small nucleolar RNA-interacting protein 2 (also known as U3-55K) from animals. Rrp9 interacts with U3 snRNP and is involved in pre-rRNA processing [[cite:PUB00089348]]. Human U3-55 protein has also been shown to bind to U3 snoRNA [[cite:PUB00089347], [cite:PUB00089346]].

Name: Apoptosis-antagonizing transcription factor, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This C-terminal domain is found in apoptosis-antagonizing transcription factor (AATF) proteins [[cite:PUB00016366]]. This is the domain of the AATF proteins that interacts with BLOS2 or Ceap, that functions as an adaptor in processes such as protein and vesicle processing and transport, and perhaps transcription.

Name: AATF leucine zipper-containing domain
ShortDescription: This leucine zipper-containing domain is found in apoptosis antagonizing transcription factor (AATF, also known as Che-1) and related proteins. AATF may function as a general inhibitor of the histone deacetylase HDAC1 [[cite:PUB00057306]]. AATF has been shown to inhibit the abberant production of the amyloid beta peptide 1-42 by direct interaction with Par4 [[cite:PUB00057401]]. This interaction occurs via the leucine zipper.

Name: Protein AATF/Bfr2
ShortDescription:
Apoptosis antagonizing transcription factor (AATF, also known as Che-1) is a adaptor that connects transcriptional regulation, cell-cycle progression, checkpoint control, and apoptosis [[cite:PUB00089516]]. It contains a leucine zipper-containing domain [[cite:PUB00057306]]. AATF has been shown to inhibit the aberrant production of the amyloid beta peptide 1-42 by direct interaction with Par4; this interaction occurs via the leucine zipper. [[cite:PUB00057401]]. AATF has also been shown to form a nucleolar protein complex with NGDN and NOL10 required for 40S ribosomal subunit synthesis [[cite:PUB00089515]].

This entry also includes the yeast protein Bfr2, which is a component of the SSU processome and 90S preribosomes [[cite:PUB00089514]].

Name: U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 4
ShortDescription: This family includes U3 small nucleolar RNA-associated protein 4 (UTP4), a ribosome biogenesis factor that is involved in nucleolar processing of pre-18S ribosomal RNA. In yeast, it is required for optimal pre-ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I [[cite:PUB00090011], [cite:PUB00035837]], while in human is required for pre-rRNA processing [[cite:PUB00093458]].

Name: Protein Cms1
ShortDescription: This family includes fungal and plant Cms1 proteins and Cmss1 (Cms1 ribosomal small subunit homologue) from metazoa. Budding yeast Cms1 may play a role in the regulation of DNA replication and cell cycle control [[cite:PUB00076759]].

Name: RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclase type 2
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the type 2 RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclases, also known as RNA'-terminal-phosphate-cyclase-like (Rcl) proteins [[cite:PUB00042947]].

;

RNA cyclases are a family of RNA-modifying enzymes that are conserved in eukaryotes, bacteria and archaea. Type 1 RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclases ([ec:6.5.1.4]) [[cite:PUB00001300], [cite:PUB00003565]] catalyse the conversion of 3'-phosphate to a 2',3'-cyclic phosphodiester at the end of RNA:

ATP + RNA 3'-terminal-phosphate = AMP + diphosphate + RNA terminal-2',3'-cyclic-phosphate

The physiological function of the cyclase is not known, but the enzyme could be involved in the maintenance of cyclic ends in tRNA splicing intermediates or in the cyclisation of the 3' end of U6 snRNA [[cite:PUB00001300]].

A second subfamily of RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclases (type 2) that do not have cyclase activity have been identified in eukaryotes. They are localised to the nucleolus and are involved in ribosomal modification [[cite:PUB00042947]].

Name: RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclase/enolpyruvate transferase, alpha/beta
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents an α/β domain consisting of alternating β-strands and α helices in two layer. This domain is found in RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclase (RPTC), where it occurs as a duplication of three repeats of this fold packed together around a pseudo three-fold axis [[cite:PUB00006476]]. RNA cyclases are a family of RNA-modifying enzymes that catalyse the ATP-dependent conversion of the 3'-phosphate to the 2',3'-cyclic phosphodiester at the end of RNA. These cyclases contain an insert α/β domain with a thioredoxin topology ([interpro:IPR013791]).

This domain is also found in enolpyruvate transferase, where it occurs as a duplication of six repeats of this fold organised into two RPTC-like domains [[cite:PUB00028019], [cite:PUB00028020]]. Enolpyruvate transferase is the first enzyme in bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis, catalysing the transfer of enolpyruvate from phosphoenolpyruvate to UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine.

ShortDescription:

RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclases contain a conserved glycine-rich stretch of residues located in the central part of the sequence, which is reminiscent of various ATP, GTP or AMP glycine-rich loops, and may be involved in AMP binding. This entry represents the conserved site.

Name: RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclase, insert domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
RNA cyclases are a family of RNA-modifying enzymes that are conserved in eukaryotes, bacteria and archaea. RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclase ([ec:6.5.1.4]) [[cite:PUB00001300], [cite:PUB00003565]] catalyses the conversion of 3'-phosphate to a 2',3'-cyclic phosphodiester at the end of RNA.

ATP + RNA 3'-terminal-phosphate = AMP + diphosphate + RNA terminal-2',3'-cyclic-phosphate

These enzymes might be responsible for production of the cyclic phosphate RNA ends that are known to be required by many RNA ligases in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

RNA cyclase is a protein of from 36 to 42kDa. The best conserved region is a glycine-rich stretch of residues located in the central part of the sequence and which is reminiscent of various ATP, GTP or AMP glycine-rich loops.

The crystal structure of RNA 3'-terminal phosphate cyclase shows that each molecule consists of two domains. The larger domain contains three repeats of a folding unit comprising two parallel α helices and a four-stranded β sheet; this fold was previously identified in translation initiation factor 3 (IF3). The large domain is similar to one of the two domains of 5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate synthase and UDP-N-acetylglucosamine enolpyruvyl transferase. The smaller insert domain disrupts the large domain, and uses a similar secondary structure element with different topology, observed in many other proteins such as thioredoxin [[cite:PUB00006476]]. Although the active site of this enzyme could not be unambiguously assigned, it can be mapped to a region surrounding His309, an adenylate acceptor, in which a number of amino acids are highly conserved in the enzyme from different sources [[cite:PUB00006476]].

This superfamily represents the small insert domain that interrupts the large repetitive domain.
